traveler: Jacobus de Voragine (Iacopo da Varazze), Order of Preachers, Archbishop of Genoa
title: The Year Laid Out as a Road: the Compiler of Saints, the Province of Lombardy, and the Burning of San Lorenzo
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: The Coast, the Habit, and the Schools

stops.name: Varazze, the name the coast gives him
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. Casagrande (DBI 62, 2004) gives 1228 or 1229 and treats the birthplace as disputed: Varazze by tradition, Genoa by her own argument, since a Genoese family called de Varagine, originating from Varazze, is separately documented in the city. Month and day unknown, defaulted to 01-01.
stops.campa: A boy is born on the Ligurian shore in a year the chroniclers can only approximate, and the little coast town of Varazze, medieval Varagine, gives him the only surname he will ever carry. Genoa disputes the cradle. A Genoese family called de Varagine, come down from the coast town into the city, is documented there, and the modern documentary life holds the city the likelier birthplace. Which of the two is right has never been settled, and the surname settles nothing, since the family carried it into Genoa with them. Nothing survives of his parents, of the household, or of the trade that fed them.
suggested_refs: The coast town of Varazze in the Riviera di Ponente, source of the toponymic surname de Varagine
sources: Carla Casagrande, 'Iacopo da Varazze', Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani vol. 62 (2004), treccani.it

stops.name: Genoa, the habit taken at fifteen
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the fact and approximate year (Casagrande, DBI 62); the exact date and the specific convent are not documented, and 'probably at Genoa' is the biographer's own hedge. Month and day defaulted to 01-01.
stops.campa: At about fifteen or sixteen he enters the Order of Preachers, probably at the Genoese convent, and this is the first thing in his life that any document will hold. Dominic has been dead twenty-three years. The order is still young, still arguing with itself about how much learning a preacher needs before he is allowed to open his mouth. No register says who brought the boy, what his family made of it, or whether he had been reading already. Behind the day there is nothing at all, and the record of his life starts here. He takes the white tunic and the black cappa.
suggested_refs: The Dominican convent of Genoa, house of his profession and of his burial seventy-four years later

stops.name: Bologna, San Domenico: grammar, logic, the Sentences
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction from the Dominican ratio studiorum, not from any register naming him at Bologna. No teacher, classroom, or year of his own formation is documented. Date chosen only to order the segment.
stops.campa: The order runs its promising men through grammar, logic, Scripture, the Sentences of Peter Lombard, theology and formal disputation, and the great study convent at Bologna is where a Lombard novice would most plausibly have taken them. He learns to divide a subject, number its parts, and preach it back. Every page he will ever write sorts its matter into fours and fives before saying anything about it at all. No register names a teacher, a room, or a year that is his. That he was at Bologna is a guess made backward from the curriculum.
suggested_refs: The Basilica di San Domenico, Bologna, principal study convent of the Lombard province
sources: Steven A. Epstein, The Talents of Jacopo da Varagine (Cornell University Press, 2016)

stops.name: Genoa, forty nights of the comet
stops.date_confidence: attested that he recorded a comet visible for forty days (Casagrande, DBI 62), year given as 1264; the place of observation is not specified and is set at his own Genoese pin. Month and day defaulted to 01-01.
stops.campa: He watches a comet burn over Italy for forty nights and writes the number down. It is the smallest surviving fact about him and the only one in which he is simply looking at something. Forty is a count he trusts: forty days of Lent, forty of the flood, forty of the desert, and now forty of a light in the sky over Liguria. The biography preserves the notice and does not preserve what he thought it meant. Whether he read it as a sign, and of what, nobody set down.
suggested_refs: The comet of 1264, one of the brightest recorded in the medieval European sky

segments.name: Legenda Sanctorum: The Year Laid Out as a Road

stops.name: Genoa, the Legenda sanctorum begun
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the work and approximately to the decade (Casagrande, DBI 62; Maggioni's critical introduction, SISMEL 1998); no start date is recorded and the place of composition is given only as Lombardy. Month and day defaulted to 01-01.
stops.campa: Around this year he begins assembling what he calls the Legenda sanctorum, the readings of the saints, following the liturgical year from Advent around to Advent again. It is a working tool and not a book for its own sake: a compact repertory a friar can carry, open at the day's feast, and preach from before breakfast. Each chapter opens with an etymology of the saint's name, then gives the life, then the doctrine the life demonstrates. Copies begin leaving his hands almost at once, and he goes on revising his own for thirty-eight years.
suggested_refs: Giovanni Paolo Maggioni, ed., Iacopo da Varazze, Legenda aurea, critical edition (Florence: SISMEL, 1998)
sources: Maggioni, ed., Legenda aurea (SISMEL, 1998), critical introduction

stops.name: Genoa, Advent: the four comings
stops.date_confidence: the text is attested (Caxton's 1483 English, ed. Ellis, Temple Classics, via the Fordham Internet Medieval Sourcebook); the date is an ordering device only, since no chapter of the Legenda can be dated within his decades of revision.
stops.campa: The book opens where the year opens, on the four weeks before the Nativity, and he begins as he will begin everything, by counting. Four comings: in the flesh, into the mind, at the hour of death, at the judgment. He is not writing history and never claims to be. He is building a machine a preacher can operate on any morning of the year, in any church in Lombardy, in front of a congregation that cannot read a word. The four weeks are hallowed, he writes, in betokening of four divers comings.
stops.quote: The time of the Advent or coming of our Lord into this world is hallowed in Holy Church the time of four weeks, in betokening of four divers comings.
stops.quote_source: Jacobus de Voragine, The Golden Legend, tr. William Caxton (1483), ed. F. S. Ellis, Temple Classics (1900), vol. 1, 'Of the Advent of our Lord'
suggested_refs: Fordham University, Internet Medieval Sourcebook, The Golden Legend, volume 1
sources: The Golden Legend, tr. Caxton, ed. Ellis, Temple Classics vol. 1, via sourcebooks.fordham.edu

stops.name: Genoa, the Nativity inside a census
stops.date_confidence: the text is attested (Caxton, ed. Ellis, vol. 1, via Fordham); the date orders the segment and does not date the chapter, which cannot be dated within the work's successive recensions.
stops.campa: For the Nativity he sets the manger inside an imperial audit. Octavian commands that all the world be described, so that he may know how many cities, how many towns, how many persons he holds; and while the empire counts, the child is born inside its arithmetic. Chronology in this book is not a problem to be solved but a figure to be stated. He dates the moment to the five thousand nine hundredth year of the world, after Eusebius the holy saint, and hedges it nowhere.
stops.quote: When the world had endured five thousand and nine hundred years, after Eusebius the holy saint, Octavian the Emperor commanded that all the world should be described, so that he might know how many cities, how many towns, and how many persons he had in all the universal world.
stops.quote_source: Jacobus de Voragine, The Golden Legend, tr. Caxton, ed. Ellis, Temple Classics (1900), vol. 1, 'The Nativity of our Lord Jesus Christ'
suggested_refs: Eusebius of Caesarea's Chronicon, the reckoning Jacobus takes his world-year from
sources: The Golden Legend, tr. Caxton, ed. Ellis, Temple Classics vol. 1, via sourcebooks.fordham.edu

stops.name: Genoa, Septuagesima: the going out of the way
stops.date_confidence: text attested (Caxton, ed. Ellis, vol. 1, via Fordham). Date is an ordering device; the chapter is undatable within the revisions.
stops.campa: Past Epiphany and the Circumcision he lays out Septuagesima, and with it the shape he gives to the whole of time. The world went out of its way at Adam and stayed out of it until Moses, and the church walks that going-out backward every spring, from deviation to renovation. He is teaching a friar how to stand inside the calendar and know, on any given morning, which century he is preaching from and what it owes. Lent begins on the Sunday whose mass sings Invocavit me.
stops.quote: Here beginneth Septuagesima. At Septuagesima beginneth the time of deviation or going out of the way, of the whole world, which began at Adam and dured unto Moses.
stops.quote_source: Jacobus de Voragine, The Golden Legend, tr. Caxton, ed. Ellis, Temple Classics (1900), vol. 1, 'Septuagesima'
suggested_refs: The Legenda's fourfold division of sacred time: deviation, renovation, reconciliation, pilgrimage
sources: The Golden Legend, tr. Caxton, ed. Ellis, Temple Classics vol. 1, via sourcebooks.fordham.edu

stops.name: Genoa, the Passion counted in five
stops.date_confidence: text attested (Caxton, ed. Ellis, vol. 1, via Fordham). Date orders the segment only.
stops.campa: Even the crucifixion is enumerated. The passion was bitter for the sorrow suffered in derisions despiteous, and the sorrow, he writes, was cause of five things. Then the five, one after another, in order, each with its authority. The counting is what makes the grief portable: a friar with no library and no education past the convent school can carry the whole of Good Friday in his head down a road between two villages and set it out again intact. He gets it in five parts.
stops.quote: The passion of our Lord was bitter for the sorrow that he suffered in derisions despitous and of many filths fructuous. The sorrow was cause of five things.
stops.quote_source: Jacobus de Voragine, The Golden Legend, tr. Caxton, ed. Ellis, Temple Classics (1900), vol. 1, 'The Passion of our Lord'
suggested_refs: The Legenda aurea as preaching aid rather than devotional reading, per Sherry L. Reames, The Legenda aurea (1985)
sources: The Golden Legend, tr. Caxton, ed. Ellis, Temple Classics vol. 1, via sourcebooks.fordham.edu
Sherry L. Reames, The Legenda aurea: A Reexamination of Its Paradoxical History (1985)

stops.name: Genoa, Christopher at the ford and George at Silene
stops.date_confidence: attested that both saints have chapters in the Legenda and that later journey files draw their narrative from it; the date orders the segment and does not date composition of either chapter.
stops.campa: Into the calendar he sets Christopher, the giant born among the dog-headed tribe of Marmarica, who carries a child across a river and feels the whole weight of the world settle onto one shoulder in midstream. And George, who rides down the dragon at the pool outside Silene and leads it into the town on the princess's own girdle. Each gets a day, an etymology, and a sequence of sentences a friar can say out loud. Neither man is documented anywhere outside books like this one, and nowhere in the chapters does Jacobus say he believes them.
suggested_refs: 'Of Saint Christopher' and 'Of Saint George, Martyr' in Caxton's Golden Legend, the source texts behind san_cristobal.journey.json and saint_george.journey.json
sources: The Golden Legend, tr. Caxton, ed. Ellis, Temple Classics, via sourcebooks.fordham.edu
san_cristobal.journey.json and saint_george.journey.json, which cite the Legenda throughout

stops.name: Genoa, Catherine's wheel, Barbara's tower, Denis walking
stops.date_confidence: attested that all three have Legenda chapters and that the corresponding journey files cite the Legenda as their narrative source; the date orders the segment only.
stops.campa: Catherine of Alexandria argues down fifty philosophers, and the wheel built to break her breaks itself instead. Barbara's father shuts her in a tower and is struck by lightning for what he does when she comes out of it. He writes all three into the same year, between the ordinary Sundays, in the same flat voice he uses for etymologies, and the book never raises its volume for a miracle. Denis, beheaded on the hill above Paris, picks up his own head and walks with it, preaching, to the ground that will take his name.
suggested_refs: The Legenda chapters on Catherine, Barbara and Denis, source texts behind catherine_alexandria.journey.json, saint_barbara.journey.json and saint_denis.journey.json
sources: The Golden Legend, tr. Caxton, ed. Ellis, Temple Classics, via sourcebooks.fordham.edu
catherine_alexandria.journey.json, saint_barbara.journey.json, saint_denis.journey.json, each citing the Legenda

stops.name: Genoa, the helpers in extremity
stops.date_confidence: attested that Blaise, Erasmus, Vitus, Eustace and Cyriacus all have Legenda chapters cited as source by their own journey files. The later grouping into the Fourteen Holy Helpers is [R]: a devotional formation of the following century, not Jacobus's own, and no journey file for the group exists in the corpus. Date orders the segment only.
stops.campa: Blaise, who takes the fishbone out of the child's throat. Erasmus, whose entrails are wound out on a windlass. Vitus, boiled and not dying. Eustace, who sees the crucifix standing between a stag's antlers and then loses everything twice over. Cyriacus, the Roman patrician who gave his property away and drove out demons afterward. Jacobus gives each of them a chapter and nowhere names them together. The company of fourteen invoked against plague is assembled out of this material in the century after he is dead.
suggested_refs: The Fourteen Holy Helpers, a later devotional grouping assembled from Legenda material; no journey file for the group exists in the corpus
sources: The Golden Legend, tr. Caxton, ed. Ellis, Temple Classics, via sourcebooks.fordham.edu
saint_blaise.journey.json, saint_erasmus.journey.json, san_vito.journey.json, saint_eustace.journey.json, saint_cyriacus.journey.json, each citing the Legenda

stops.name: Genoa, the Magdalene given Provence
stops.date_confidence: attested that the Legenda carries the Provencal legend and that mary_magdalene.journey.json cites it for the post-Gospel arc; the legend predates Jacobus and he is its transmitter, not its inventor. Date orders the segment only.
stops.campa: For the twenty-second of July he gives Mary Magdalene a second life the Gospels never mention. Set adrift from Palestine in a boat with no rudder and no oar, landed at Marseille, preaching to the Provencals, thirty years alone in a cave in the mountain, carried up by angels at each of the seven hours to hear what is sung above. The story is older than him and he did not invent it. He fixed it, and after the Legenda this is what Europe knows about her for three hundred years. Where he took it from, and from which of the versions then circulating, he does not say.
suggested_refs: 'Of Saint Mary Magdalene' in Caxton's Golden Legend, source text behind mary_magdalene.journey.json
sources: The Golden Legend, tr. Caxton, ed. Ellis, Temple Classics, via sourcebooks.fordham.edu
mary_magdalene.journey.json, citing the Legenda for the Provencal legend

stops.name: Asti, the priorate a chronicle asserts
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction, weakly supported. Only Girolamo Albertucci de' Borselli's fifteenth-century Dominican chronicle names him prior at Asti in 1266, and Casagrande flags the whole series of early priorates as unproven. No Asti document has been located. Month and day defaulted to 01-01.
stops.campa: A Dominican chronicler writing two centuries after the fact, Girolamo Albertucci de' Borselli, makes him prior at Asti in this year, and prior at Como and at Bologna before that. Three priorates rest on that one late memory. The Legenda's chapter on Secundus, patron of Asti, is the only circumstantial support anyone has offered, and it supports nothing at all: he wrote chapters on the saints of towns he never went near. No Asti document has been found.
suggested_refs: Girolamo Albertucci de' Borselli, Cronica magistrorum generalium ordinis fratrum praedicatorum (15th c.), the sole source for the early priorates
sources: Casagrande, DBI 62 (2004), treccani.it, flagging the priorates as unproven

stops.name: Bologna, the general chapter elects him provincial
stops.date_confidence: attested (Casagrande, DBI 62; Wikipedia). Year certain, exact chapter date not given in the sources consulted; month set to the usual Pentecost season of a general chapter.
stops.campa: The general chapter meeting at Bologna elects him prior provincial of Lombardy. The province runs from the Alps down through Emilia to the March of Ancona, dozens of houses, and the office is mostly travel: visitation, correction, the settling of quarrels between convents, attendance at chapters that meet in a different city every year. For the next ten years the friar compiling a book about the saints spends his working life on the roads of northern Italy, auditing convents. He is not yet forty.
suggested_refs: The Dominican province of Lombardy, spanning northern Italy, Emilia and the March of Ancona

stops.name: Milan, Sant'Eustorgio: the province governed
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The office is attested for 1267-1277; Sant'Eustorgio is named only as one of the province's likeliest operational houses, and no itinerary or residence pattern survives. Date chosen to sit inside the term.
stops.campa: Sant'Eustorgio in Milan is one of the great houses of the Lombard province and among the likeliest places from which a provincial would govern it. What is documented is the office and its duties; through the whole decade the man himself moves as a title, visiting houses the record does not name. No itinerary survives. Not a night's lodging, not a route between two convents, not one dated letter putting him in a particular refectory on a particular evening across ten years in office.
suggested_refs: The Basilica di Sant'Eustorgio, Milan, principal Dominican house of the city
sources: Casagrande, DBI 62 (2004), treccani.it, on the province's major houses

stops.name: Bordeaux, absolutus
stops.date_confidence: attested (Casagrande, DBI 62; Wikipedia). Year certain; exact chapter date not given, month set to the general chapter season.
stops.campa: At the general chapter held in Bordeaux he is absolutus, released from the provincialate. The Latin carries no verdict in it. Dominican usage releases men from office as a matter of course, and no scandal, trial or finding of any kind attaches to this one in a surviving act. Ten years in and out of every convent between Ancona and the Alps end at a chapter in Gascony. He is about forty-nine, and he goes home to Lombardy with no charge standing against him. Why he was released, no surviving act says.
suggested_refs: The Dominican general chapter of Bordeaux, 1277

stops.name: Genoa, the years out of office
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction (Casagrande, DBI 62): the interval 1277-1281 is attested, the preaching, teaching and revising are inferred from his output and from the work's known recensions. Date chosen to sit inside the interval.
stops.campa: Four years with no office. He preaches, he teaches, and he keeps working at the Legenda, which by now is copying itself faster than he can amend it. Friars add local saints. Scribes drop chapters that do not suit their house. Recensions multiply in convents he will never see. He goes on correcting his own copy regardless, as though corrections could catch up with copies. Seven centuries later Maggioni is still separating the author's successive hands from everyone else's.
suggested_refs: The successive authorial recensions of the Legenda aurea, reconstructed in Maggioni's 1998 critical edition

stops.name: Bologna, restored to the province
stops.date_confidence: attested (Casagrande, DBI 62; Wikipedia): the provincial chapter at Bologna restores him in 1281. Exact date not given; month and day defaulted to 01-01.
stops.campa: The provincial chapter at Bologna puts him back. Whatever the release of 1277 had meant, it did not mean disgrace: the same province returns him to the same office after four years out, by the vote of the same kind of assembly that let him go. He is in his early fifties, and he has been governing or writing without pause since he was under forty. Nothing in the vote at Bologna, so far as any surviving act shows, anticipates trouble. The second term will run five years and will end in a quarrel that reaches the papal curia.
suggested_refs: The Lombard provincial chapter of 1281

segments.name: Relics, and an Order Without a Head

stops.name: Cologne, the head of one of Ursula's virgins
stops.date_confidence: attested that the relic came from Cologne before Easter 1283 (his own Historia reliquiarum, via Casagrande, DBI 62); whether he travelled there himself is not stated in the sources consulted, and no other journey file in the corpus carries a Cologne pin, so this one is newly set at the Basilica of St. Ursula rather than inherited. Exact date unknown.
stops.campa: He arranges for a head to be brought south out of Cologne: one of the eleven thousand virgins said to have been killed with Ursula outside the walls, whose bones the city has been unearthing and distributing across Europe for a century. The Historia reliquiarum he writes afterward records the transfer and does not describe him standing in the shrine. A relic moves the length of the continent and arrives. Did he cross the Alps to fetch it, or send? The document does not say, and nothing else in the record answers it.
suggested_refs: The Basilica of St. Ursula, Cologne, and its Golden Chamber of the eleven thousand virgins
sources: Jacobus de Voragine, Historia reliquiarum que sunt in monasterio sororum Sanctorum Philippi et Iacobi de Ianua, as summarized in Casagrande, DBI 62 (2004)

stops.name: Genoa, Saints Philip and James: the relic installed on Easter
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the act and to Easter Day 1283 (Historia reliquiarum, via Casagrande); the sources consulted give the feast, not a calendar date, so the day is defaulted to 04-01. The convent no longer stands and its site is only approximately fixed. The quoted rubric describes him as former prior provincial, so the text was written after 1286, later than the event it records.
stops.campa: On Easter Day the Cologne relic is installed at the Dominican women's convent of Saints Philip and James in Genoa, a house he has already given a finger said to be Philip the Apostle's. The convent is gone now and its plan is unrecovered; what survives of it is a list of what it held, kept by the man who put part of the list there. He writes that account years after the fact. Its opening rubric calls him quondam priorem provincialem, former prior provincial, an office he still held on the Easter Day it describes.
stops.quote: Incipit historia reliquiarum [...] compilata per fratrem Jacobum de Varagine quondam priorem provincialem
stops.quote_source: Jacobus de Voragine, Historia reliquiarum que sunt in monasterio sororum Sanctorum Philippi et Iacobi de Ianua, opening rubric, quoted in Casagrande, DBI 62 (2004)
suggested_refs: The Dominican women's convent of Saints Philip and James, Genoa, no longer standing
sources: Jacobus de Voragine, Historia reliquiarum, as quoted and summarized in Casagrande, DBI 62 (2004)

stops.name: Genoa, the Order without a master
stops.date_confidence: attested by Casagrande (DBI 62), who has him acting as regent of the order 1283-1285; the exact constitutional title, and where he exercised it, are not fixed in the sources. John of Vercelli died 30 November 1283 at Montpellier; Munio de Zamora was elected at the general chapter of Bologna in 1285.
stops.campa: John of Vercelli, master general for nineteen years, dies at Montpellier on the last day of November, and the Order of Preachers has no head. The documentary life has Jacobus governing it in the interval, regent or vicar, until the chapter at Bologna elects Munio de Zamora eighteen months later. For a year and a half he runs the Order of Preachers. What his title was in that time is fixed nowhere, and no one recorded where he sat while he held it.
suggested_refs: The Dominican interregnum of 1283-1285, between John of Vercelli and Munio de Zamora
sources: Wikipedia, 'John of Vercelli' and 'Munio of Zamora' for the death at Montpellier and the Bologna election

stops.name: Bologna, the second term ends
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction as to manner and place. That the second provincialate ended in 1286 is attested; summaries diverge on whether he was released at a meeting in Paris or simply completed the term at a Lombard chapter, and Casagrande notes the divergence without resolving it. Pinned at Bologna as the province's usual chapter seat.
stops.campa: His second provincialate ends. The summaries disagree about how. Some have him released at a meeting in Paris; others have him simply serving the term out at a Lombard chapter, and no act settles it either way. Nothing financial and nothing criminal is attached to the change anywhere in the record. He stays in the province's business afterward as a definitor, which is the kind of thing a man keeps doing when he has not left office badly. He is about fifty-eight.
suggested_refs: The divergence in the sources over where the second provincialate ended, Paris or Lombardy, unresolved

segments.name: The Curia, the Deposition, and a Mitre in an Empty See

stops.name: Lucca, named diffinitor at the general chapter
stops.date_confidence: attested. Casagrande (DBI 62) has him named diffinitor at the general chapter of Lucca in 1288; some summaries call it a provincial chapter, which is wrong. Exact date not given; month set to the general chapter season.
stops.campa: He is named diffinitor at the general chapter of Lucca, one of the men who sit with the master general and settle the order's legislation for the year. It is a place of trust given to a former provincial who is no longer provincial, and it puts him back at the centre of the order's business without any office to run. After this year his career stops being internal to the Dominicans. He is about sixty, and the papacy is about to find work for him in his own city.
suggested_refs: The Dominican general chapter of Lucca, 1288

stops.name: Genoa, absolving the city, and the mitre that does not come
stops.date_confidence: both facts attested for 1288 (Casagrande, DBI 62; Wikipedia): the papal faculty to absolve the Genoese, and the failed candidacy for the archbishopric. Exact dates not given, and the order between them within the year is not established. Month and day chosen only to place the stop.
stops.campa: Nicholas IV empowers him to absolve the Genoese for having backed the Sicilians against Charles II of Anjou. Six years after the Vespers a whole commune is still under censure, and the power to lift it is handed to a Dominican friar of that same commune. In the same year the see of Genoa falls vacant, he is put forward for it, and he fails to get a majority; the archbishopric goes elsewhere and he is given administrative work instead. He absolves the city that has just declined to elect him.
suggested_refs: The aftermath of the Sicilian Vespers of 1282 and the Genoese censure lifted in 1288

stops.name: Ferrara, the demand that a master resign
stops.date_confidence: attested that the 1290 general chapter met at Ferrara and that Jacobus was there (Casagrande, DBI 62). The detail that he was one of four papally aligned delegates charged with conveying Nicholas IV's demand rests on Wikipedia alone and is hedged; the Wikipedia article on Munio has him re-elected at the 1290 chapter and does not mention the delegation.
stops.campa: At the general chapter of Ferrara the pope's demand arrives: Munio de Zamora, master of the Order of Preachers, is to resign. Later accounts make Jacobus one of four delegates charged with carrying that demand to him, though the point rests on thin sourcing and one account has Munio re-elected at this same chapter. Jacobus is on the pope's side against his own order. Munio refuses to go. Nicholas IV deprives him by bull the following April, and the bull is seized in Spain before it can be read out.
suggested_refs: The bull of 12 April 1291 depriving Munio de Zamora, sent to the general chapter then meeting at Palencia and seized there
sources: Casagrande, DBI 62 (2004), treccani.it, for the Ferrara general chapter
Wikipedia, 'Jacobus de Voragine' for the four delegates; Wikipedia, 'Munio of Zamora' for the 1291 bull and its seizure at Palencia

stops.name: Ferrara, the well
stops.date_confidence: tradition, rejected by the modern documentary life. Only Borselli's fifteenth-century chronicle reports the attempt, Casagrande doubts it, and nothing contemporary corroborates it. Date set immediately after the chapter for ordering.
stops.campa: Borselli's chronicle, written two hundred years later, says his brothers in religion tried to throw him down a well at Ferrara. Nothing contemporary says anything of the kind, and the modern documentary life treats the story as not worth believing. What it preserves is not an event but a fifteenth-century Dominican's sense of how bitter the year 1290 had been inside the order, and of what a friar taking the pope's part might have had coming to him from his own house. The chronicle names no well and gives no day.
suggested_refs: Borselli's chronicle, the sole and late witness to both attempts on his life
sources: Girolamo Albertucci de' Borselli, Dominican chronicle (15th c.), as reported and doubted in Casagrande, DBI 62 (2004)

stops.name: Milan, Stefanardo excluded
stops.date_confidence: tradition, same single late source. Borselli reports both the exclusion of Stefanardo, prior of Milan, from a provincial chapter and a second attempt on Jacobus's life at Milan; Casagrande doubts it and nothing contemporary corroborates. Pinned at Sant'Eustorgio, the city's Dominican house. Exact date unknown.
stops.campa: He excludes Stefanardo, prior of Milan, from a provincial chapter, and the same fifteenth-century chronicle reports a second attempt on his life there as the consequence. Nothing contemporary corroborates it, exactly as at Ferrara. Two attempted murders, one source, two hundred years late, and total silence from every register and act of the years themselves. Either the career made enemies whom the documents decline to name, or a chronicler liked the shape of a pattern and supplied its second half.
suggested_refs: Stefanardo, prior of the Dominican convent of Milan, excluded from a provincial chapter
sources: Borselli, Dominican chronicle (15th c.), as reported and doubted in Casagrande, DBI 62 (2004)

stops.name: Rome, summoned, and the pope dies
stops.date_confidence: attested. Wikipedia gives Palm Sunday, 30 March 1292, for his arrival; Nicholas IV's death on 4 April 1292 is attested in both Casagrande and Wikipedia. Where he lodged in Rome is not recorded.
stops.campa: Nicholas IV summons him to Rome intending to consecrate him archbishop of Genoa with his own hands. He reaches the city around Palm Sunday, in the week the church walks toward a death. On the fourth of April the pope dies, and there is nobody left with authority to finish what was arranged. The cardinals go into a conclave that will run more than two years. Jacobus is in Rome, named to a see, unconsecrated, in a church with no head, and the sources do not say where he slept.
suggested_refs: The papal vacancy of April 1292 to July 1294, one of the longest in the church's history
sources: Wikipedia, 'Jacobus de Voragine', giving Palm Sunday as 30 March 1292

stops.name: Rome, consecrated in the empty see
stops.date_confidence: attested (Casagrande, DBI 62; Wikipedia): consecrated 13 April 1292 by Cardinal Latino Malabranca Orsini, bishop of Ostia, during the vacancy, 'for the honor of the commune of Genoa'. The church in which it took place is not named in the sources consulted.
stops.campa: Nine days after the pope's death, with the see of Peter empty and no successor in prospect, Cardinal Latino Malabranca Orsini, bishop of Ostia and himself a Dominican, consecrates him archbishop of Genoa. The stated reason is the honor of the commune of Genoa. It is irregular in its timing and completely open; no source calls it secret. A cardinal acting in a vacancy makes a bishop for the city that had declined to elect him four years earlier. Which church it happened in, nobody wrote down.
suggested_refs: Cardinal Latino Malabranca Orsini, bishop of Ostia, Dominican, consecrator during the 1292 vacancy

stops.name: Sanremo, the archbishop as temporal lord
stops.date_confidence: attested that the see held temporal lordship over Sanremo across his episcopate (Casagrande, DBI 62); no document places him personally in the town, and the date marks the start of the archiepiscopate rather than any recorded visit.
stops.campa: The archbishop of Genoa is a temporal lord, and Sanremo on the western Riviera is one of the places he now rules: rents, courts, appointments, the ordinary weight of a signory hung on a mitre. He did not seek it and he cannot put it down. Nothing in the record suggests he ever spent much time there, or any time at all. The collectors and the vicars go, the accounts come back to the palace at Genoa, and what the town gets of its lord is a jurisdiction exercised at a distance. In five years he will sell it.
suggested_refs: The temporal signories of the archbishopric of Genoa on the Riviera di Ponente

stops.name: Ceriana, the hill town under the crozier
stops.date_confidence: attested that the see held Ceriana (Casagrande, DBI 62); no visit is documented. Coordinates corrected to the town itself, 43.883 / 7.767, against an erroneous value circulating in the research pool. Date marks the episcopate, not an event.
stops.campa: Inland from Sanremo, up the valley, the hill town of Ceriana is likewise held by the see. Between the Legenda and the chronicle he has not yet begun, between provincial chapters and a cathedral that has not yet burned, the archbishop of Genoa is also the landlord of two small Ligurian communities who owe him money every year. The office reaches a good deal further into Liguria than the man himself ever does. Rents come down the valley to Genoa; no document puts him in the streets of either town.
suggested_refs: Ceriana, Province of Imperia, signory of the archbishopric until 1297

stops.name: Genoa, San Lorenzo: the council and the bones of Syrus
stops.date_confidence: the provincial council of June 1293 is attested (Casagrande, DBI 62); the recognition of the bones of Syrus and the Vita sancti Syri written for the occasion are [R], resting on the Legenda seu Vita sancti Syri ed. Promis (1874) as characterized by Casagrande. Exact day not given.
stops.campa: In his own cathedral he holds a provincial council: bishops, clergy, the civic authorities, an attempt to put the whole Genoese church under one discipline. In the course of it officials open a tomb and inspect bones attributed to Syrus, the early bishop and patron of the city, and pronounce them authentic, first before the rulers and then before the assembled people. Thirty years of compiling other men's saints, and here he is certifying one. For the occasion he writes a life of Syrus, which Promis will print in 1874.
suggested_refs: Legenda seu Vita sancti Syri episcopi Ianuensis, ed. Vincenzo Promis (1874)
sources: Jacobus de Voragine, Vita sancti Syri, ed. Promis (1874), as characterized in the DBI

stops.name: Genoa, the archbishop writing in the episcopal mirror
stops.date_confidence: the Liber Marialis and the prologue phrase are attested through Casagrande's DBI, which quotes the prologue; the edition itself was not consulted and the DBI stands as an intermediary source. The composition is not precisely datable within the episcopate, and the date orders the segment.
stops.campa: He is still writing, and the archbishopric has not stopped it. Beside the Legenda he assembles a Mariale, hundreds of sermons on the Virgin, put together in the years he is governing the diocese. The compiler who spent thirty years standing behind other people's lives has become a life other people read, and the prologue does not say whether he wanted that. It says only where he now stands: in episcopali speculo constitutus, set up in an episcopal mirror, looked into by everyone he governs.
stops.quote_source: Jacobus de Voragine, Liber Marialis, prologue, quoted in Casagrande, DBI 62 (2004), treccani.it
suggested_refs: The Liber Marialis (Mariale), his collection of Marian sermons written as archbishop
sources: Casagrande, DBI 62 (2004), treccani.it, quoting the Mariale prologue

stops.name: Genoa, the peace between mascherati and rampini
stops.date_confidence: attested (Casagrande, DBI 62; Wikipedia) to the first months of 1295; no exact date is given, and the month is set from 'the first months of the year'.
stops.campa: In the first months of the year he preaches in the open air, leads the clergy in praise, and walks a solemn procession through the city to reconcile the Ghibelline mascherati and the Guelf rampini. He is sixty-seven years old. The factions come to terms. For one season Genoa has an archbishop who has stopped a civil war with a sermon and a parade, and afterward some in the city call him father of the fatherland. Nothing else he did there was received like this. The peace lasts less than a year.
suggested_refs: The Genoese factions of the 1290s, the Ghibelline mascherati and the Guelf rampini

stops.name: Genoa, San Lorenzo burns
stops.date_confidence: attested that the peace collapsed late in 1295 and that renewed factional violence badly damaged San Lorenzo by fire, with his own lament preserved in the Chronica via Casagrande. Exact date not given. The papal compensation of 12 June 1296 is carried in the pool from the dossier's synthesis and was not independently confirmed.
stops.campa: The peace does not hold the year out. Factional fighting resumes, fire takes the cathedral of San Lorenzo, and the building he had preached the reconciliation in is left badly damaged. The following June, papal authority grants some compensation for what was lost. Writing his own chronicle of the city, the archbishop reaches for Job and Lamentations and does not explain the year away or assign it to providence: cithara nostra cito versa est in luctum, our harp was quickly turned to mourning.
stops.quote: cithara nostra cito versa est in luctum et organum nostrum in voce flentium est mutatum
stops.quote_source: Jacobus de Voragine, Chronica civitatis Ianuensis, quoted in Casagrande, DBI 62 (2004), treccani.it. Literal gloss: 'our harp was quickly turned to mourning and our organ changed into the voice of those who weep'
suggested_refs: The Cattedrale di San Lorenzo, Genoa, damaged by fire in the factional violence of late 1295
sources: Casagrande, DBI 62 (2004), treccani.it, quoting the Chronica

stops.name: Genoa, the Chronica of the city
stops.date_confidence: attested. Wikipedia dates composition 1295-1298; the work runs to 1297 and is edited by Giovanni Monleone (Rome, 1941). Date chosen inside the composition window. The Doria phrase is quoted through Casagrande, an intermediary; the Chronica itself was not consulted directly.
stops.campa: In the archiepiscopal palace he writes the Chronica civitatis Ianuensis: twelve parts, from the founding of Genoa by two men named Janus down to his own worst year, closing with a catalogue of everything he has ever written. He gives the city its origin myth and its recent history in one volume, and ends it with an inventory of his own writing. Oberto Doria comes home from a naval expedition and is received, he writes, cum immenso gaudio et triumpho. The chronicle stops at 1297. He has a year left.
stops.quote_source: Jacobus de Voragine, Chronica civitatis Ianuensis, on Oberto Doria's return, quoted in Casagrande, DBI 62 (2004), treccani.it
suggested_refs: Giovanni Monleone, Iacopo da Varagine e la sua Cronaca di Genova (Rome, 1941); Carrie E. Benes, tr., Jacopo da Varagine's Chronicle of the City of Genoa (Manchester University Press, 2019)

stops.name: Sanremo, the signories sold
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1297 that Sanremo went to Oberto Doria and Ceriana to Giorgio De Mari (Casagrande, DBI 62, and the research pool's synthesis of Genoese notarial records); the underlying notarial acts were not read directly, and the devotional claim that the proceeds went to the poor is unverified. Exact date unknown.
stops.campa: He sells the signory of Sanremo to Oberto Doria and that of Ceriana to Giorgio De Mari, and the see is out of the business of ruling hill towns. Both buyers come from Ghibelline-associated houses; the archbishop who could not hold the peace between the factions has sold two towns to one side of it. Later devotional accounts say the money went to the poor. Nobody who says so has produced the notarial acts that would show it, and nobody has produced evidence of profit or fraud either.
suggested_refs: Genoese notarial records of the 1297 alienation of Sanremo and Ceriana
sources: research pool synthesis of Genoese notarial documentation, not independently verified

stops.name: Genoa, the final notarial acts
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. That notarial acts of his last months set out directions for the archdiocese and confirmed an earlier testament comes through the research pool's synthesis of the archiepiscopal record and was not independently confirmed; exact dates unknown.
stops.campa: Notarial acts of his last months record instructions for the management of the archdiocese and confirm a testament made earlier. He is about seventy. The documents are entirely ordinary: a bishop putting an office in order, not a man composing a deathbed. This is the last stretch of paper he generates while alive, and it is administrative. Nothing in it shows enrichment, and nobody has produced a Genoese act that does. Nothing in it names an illness.
suggested_refs: Genoese notarial acts of 1298 concerning the archdiocese and his testament
sources: research pool synthesis of Genoese notarial acts, characterized but not independently verified

stops.name: Genoa, the night of the thirteenth
stops.date_confidence: attested (Wikipedia; corroborated by Casagrande, DBI 62): death in the night of 13-14 July 1298. Some older reference works give 1299, and some give 16 July; 1298 and the night of 13-14 July are the better supported, and the divergence is recorded rather than resolved.
stops.campa: He dies in Genoa in the night between the thirteenth and the fourteenth of July. No cause is preserved: no illness named, no accident, no deathbed scene, nothing but a night and the two dates it falls between. He has been archbishop for six years and has been revising the same book for thirty-eight. Some older reference works give 1299 instead, and some the sixteenth of July; the sources have not been reconciled and are not reconciled here. The thirteenth becomes his feast at Genoa, at Savona, and through the Order of Preachers.
suggested_refs: The divergence in reference works over the year (1298 or 1299) and the day (13-14 or 16 July)

stops.name: Genoa, San Domenico: the effigy and the lost tomb
stops.date_confidence: the burial at San Domenico is attested (Casagrande; Wikipedia). The exact burial date is not recorded and is set two days after death. The effigy is attested by the Musei di Genova catalogue, carved after 1298 by a sculptor of the 'Maestro degli angeli del Duomo' circle; its sarcophagus is lost.
stops.campa: They bury him in the Dominican church of San Domenico, the house he had entered as a boy of fifteen and governed twice as provincial. The church does not survive either: suppressed and pulled down, it becomes the ground under the Piazza De Ferrari, and nothing above it says what it was. The sarcophagus is lost too. What is left is the white marble effigy carved for the tomb, an archbishop lying mitred, hands crossed on his chest, the tip of the nose broken away at some point nobody recorded.
suggested_refs: Musei di Genova catalogue, statua giacente di Jacopo da Varagine, arcivescovo di Genova, now in the Museo di Sant'Agostino
sources: Musei di Genova online catalogue, entry 198057

segments.name: After: The Body, the Cult, and the Press

stops.name: Westminster, Caxton prints The Golden Legende
stops.date_confidence: attested (Catholic Encyclopedia, newadvent.org): Caxton's English Golden Legende, Westminster, 1483. Exact day not given. The edition counts by 1500 are the Catholic Encyclopedia's; the first Latin printing of 1470 is placed at Basle by New Advent and at Cologne by Treccani, a contradiction left open. Manuscript counts range from about 900 to over 1,400 depending on the source and what is counted.
stops.campa: William Caxton prints The Golden Legende at Westminster, the first English version, and a friar's pocket repertory becomes an object of the new machine. By 1500 there are seventy-four Latin editions, three English, five French, eight Italian, fourteen Low German, three Bohemian. Between 1470 and 1530 nothing printed in Europe sells like it. The surviving manuscripts are counted at nine hundred, or over a thousand, or over twelve hundred, depending on who is counting and what they agree to count.
suggested_refs: Caxton's Golden Legende, Westminster 1483; Theodor Graesse's Latin edition, Leipzig 1846, standard for over 150 years
sources: Fordham Internet Medieval Sourcebook, Voragine introduction

stops.name: Genoa, Santa Maria di Castello: the body moved
stops.date_confidence: attested that after San Domenico's suppression the body went to Santa Maria di Castello, dated 1798 by santiebeati.it, which also reports an intervening 1582 translation to San Domenico's high altar that Treccani does not mention. Contested: Treccani (2004) says the body is there still, while the Italian Wikipedia articles on the church and on Iacopo say it left definitively in 1974 for Varazze. Not resolved.
stops.campa: After San Domenico is suppressed and pulled down, the body is carried across the old town to Santa Maria di Castello. The documentary life written in 2004 says it is there still. Two Italian-language sources say it left in 1974 for the coast. Both cannot be right and neither has been set aside. The effigy took a road of its own and lies now in the Museo di Sant'Agostino, an archbishop in state in a museum with the tomb gone from underneath him. Where the body is, the printed record does not agree.
suggested_refs: Santa Maria di Castello, Genoa; the Museo di Sant'Agostino, holding the recumbent effigy
sources: Casagrande, DBI 62 (2004), treccani.it, 'dove tuttora si trova'
santiebeati.it, entry 62400, dating the transfer to 1798
it.wikipedia, 'Santa Maria di Castello' and 'Iacopo da Varazze', giving a definitive 1974 transfer to Varazze

stops.name: Rome, Pius VII confirms the cult
stops.date_confidence: the confirmatio cultus of 1816 is attested by Treccani, santiebeati.it and the Catholic Encyclopedia, which all give only the year; the day, 11 May, rests on Wikipedia alone. Fordham's Internet Medieval Sourcebook gives 1896, contradicting three other sources, and is treated here as an error but recorded. Placed at Rome, the issuing curia, correcting a Genoa value in the research pool.
stops.campa: Five hundred and eighteen years after his death, Pius VII confirms a cult Liguria has been keeping without interruption and without ever having been given permission for it. The act is a confirmatio cultus, an equipollent beatification: not a canonization but a ratification of what people had already been doing for centuries. The pope permits the clergy of Genoa and Savona and the whole Order of Preachers to keep his feast on the thirteenth of July.
suggested_refs: Confirmatio cultus of 1816; the feast kept on 13 July by Genoa, Savona and the Dominican Order
sources: Wikipedia, 'Jacobus de Voragine' for the day

stops.name: Varazze, San Domenico: the urn in the fifth chapel
stops.date_confidence: attested that relics are venerated at San Domenico in Varazze (santiebeati.it; it.wikipedia, which describes an urn of bones and ashes in the fifth chapel on the left). Whether this is a portion of the relics or the body itself is exactly the contested point at the previous stop. The 1974 date follows it.wikipedia and is not carried by Treccani. Coordinates corrected to the church, against two divergent values in the research pool.
stops.campa: In the church of San Domenico at Varazze, the town that gave him his surname, an urn in the fifth chapel on the left holds bones and ashes venerated as his. Whether this is a portion of the relics or the whole body depends on which source is believed, and the sources do not agree. The town keeps him in street names, in periodic historical conferences, in walking itineraries. Whoever comes looking for him finds the fifth chapel on the left and the urn standing in it. Varazze has raised him no statue.
suggested_refs: The fifth chapel on the left, San Domenico, Varazze; St Catherine of Siena is recorded there on 3 October 1376 honoring his remains (it.wikipedia), an engagement belonging to her own itinerary
sources: it.wikipedia, 'Chiesa di San Domenico (Varazze)' and 'Iacopo da Varazze'
Comune di Varazze, official page on Jacopo da Varagine
